text: STIX, short for Structured Threat Information eXpression, is a standard maintained by OASIS that defines a consistent JSON structure for describing threat intelligence -- indicators, malware families, threat actors, and how they relate. The key thing to internalize is that STIX is a format, not a specific feed or tool. Commercial platforms, government programs, and open-source feeds all produce data in STIX format, the same way many applications produce data in CSV format.

Three object types come up constantly. An indicator is a pattern that, if observed, suggests malicious activity -- its pattern field is written in a small structured language called STIX Patterning, not free text. A malware object describes a malware family or instance. A threat-actor object describes a person, group, or organization believed responsible for malicious activity, often with a sophistication rating. Every STIX object shares a common shape: a type, a unique id, and created and modified timestamps.

Look closely at an indicator's pattern field -- something like square bracket ipv4-addr colon value equals a quoted IP address, closing bracket. That's a tiny structured language in its own right, and more complex patterns combine conditions with boolean operators. Objects are usually distributed together inside a bundle -- a container with a type of bundle and a list of objects, each carrying its own unique id in the form type dash dash uuid.

STIX objects rarely stand alone -- a separate relationship object links them, expressing something like this indicator indicates this malware, through source_ref and target_ref fields pointing at other objects' ids. To make sense of a bundle in Python, you build a lookup dictionary keyed by id, then walk every relationship object, resolving source_ref and target_ref against it to print a human-readable sentence. That index-then-resolve pattern is the core of almost any STIX-processing script.

TAXII, Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information, is a separate standard defining how STIX data actually gets shared over HTTP -- a client-server API for discovering and pulling collections of STIX objects. The relationship is simple: STIX is what you're sharing, TAXII is how you ask for it. A TAXII server exposes discovery and collection endpoints over REST, and a client authenticates, finds available collections, and pulls STIX bundles from them.

For now, the important distinction is that a TAXII request's response body is just STIX JSON, parsed exactly the way you parsed the bundle earlier in this lesson. Next lesson, you'll build the real REST call patterns -- authentication, pagination, and rate limits -- that make calls like that actually work reliably in production, instead of failing the first time an API throttles you or paginates its results.
